question: Two resistors named R1 and R2, are connected in parallel. If R1 < R2, what can be inferred about the current flowing through them, given the same potential difference across both?

options.text: R1 is less than through R2.
Current through R1 is equal to current through R2.
Current through R1 is greater than through R2.
The current ratio depends on the supply voltage.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Current through R1 is greater than through R2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When resistors are connected in parallel, the **potential difference across each resistor is the same**.
 
• The current through a resistor in a parallel circuit is inversely proportional to its resistance, following Ohm's Law (**I = V/R**).
 
• Since **R1 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ohm's Law:**

 
 
• Ohm's Law states that the current (I) through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance (R).
 
• Mathematically: **I = V/R**.
 
 
 
• **Parallel Circuit Characteristics:**
 
 
• In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is the same.
 
• The total current is the sum of the currents through all the parallel branches.
 
• The effective resistance (Req) is always less than the smallest individual resistance: **1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...**
 
 
 
• **Resistance and Current Relation:**
 
 
• Resistance opposes the flow of electric current; lower resistance allows higher current.
 
• In parallel circuits, a branch with lower resistance carries more current.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Parallel Circuits:**
 
 
• Used in household wiring to ensure each appliance operates independently.
 
• Common in electrical distribution systems to distribute power efficiently.
